rules.text: Bank above 45°, or pitch above 25° up or 13° down: the PFD keeps only attitude, speed, speed trend, heading, altitude and vertical speed. It returns below 40° of bank and below 22° up or 10° down.
Beyond 30° of pitch, large red arrowheads on the pitch scale point the way to move the nose.
Green = marks show the bank (67°) and pitch (30° up, 15° down) protections. An amber x replaces them when the protection is lost, as in alternate and direct law.
The yellow sideslip index under the roll index shows sideslip; 1 cm of travel is 0.2 g and it stops at 0.3 g.
Alternate or direct law with more than 45° of bank: BANK BANK on both PFDs and the "BANK BANK" aural.

Angle of attack above the warning threshold: red STALL STALL on the PFD, one word either side of the centre, with the "STALL, STALL" voice and the cricket. MASTER WARN flashes red while the warning lasts.
Direct law or the abnormal attitude law: USE MAN PITCH TRIM in amber on the FMA; pitch trim is manual.

Beyond 40° up or 20° down (50° or 30° with two valid ADCs), 125° of bank, 40° of angle of attack, 440 kt or M .91, the abnormal attitude law engages: pitch alternate with no protection and no autotrim, roll direct, yaw mechanical, and F/CTL DIRECT LAW on the ECAM with MASTER CAUT and a single chime. When it disengages, alternate law without reduced protection, roll direct, stays for the rest of the flight, with F/CTL ALTN LAW on the ECAM: a new amber caution, so MASTER CAUT and a single chime again.
G LOAD in amber on the SD when the load factor is above 1.4 g or below 0.7 g for more than 2 s; it stays 5 s after.

Speed scale: yellow 10 s speed trend arrow, amber VLS strip, amber and black α prot strip and red α max strip in normal law, red and black VSW strip in alternate and direct law, red and black VMAX strip, green = speed protection symbol at VMO + 6 kt or MMO + 0.01 in normal law, green dot in clean configuration.

Above VMO + 4 kt or MMO + 0.006 (VLE + 4 kt with the gear down, VFE + 4 kt with slats or flaps out): the red OVERSPEED warning, with the continuous repetitive chime and MASTER WARN flashing. Pressing MASTER WARN does not stop it.
Alpha floor (normal law, below M 0.6): TOGA thrust whatever the thrust levers and the A/THR status. A.FLOOR in green in a flashing amber box on the FMA, A/THR active, and A.FLOOR on the EWD.

Above 20 000 ft VLS keeps a 0.2 g margin from the buffet, and α prot falls with Mach so that it protects from the buffet boundary. The books give no buffet chart: buffet, α prot and α max at high Mach are illustrative.

ILS raw data, once the LS pushbutton is pressed: the localizer scale under the attitude sphere and the glideslope scale on its right, white dots at one and two dots and a magenta diamond for each deviation. One dot is 0.8° on the localizer and 0.4° on the glideslope; beyond two dots only half a diamond shows, at the end of the scale. The ILS ident, frequency and DME distance show bottom left, and a magenta dagger on the heading scale marks the ILS course.
Radio height below 2 500 ft, under the attitude sphere: green, and amber at 400 ft or below when no decision height is entered. It changes every 10 ft down to 50 ft.

exercises.title: Roll Rate with full Aileron/Spoiler Input

form.title: Roll Rate with full Aileron/Spoiler Input

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: Roll to 60⁰ of a bank, neutralize the controls at 60⁰, then rapidly roll in the opposite direction to 60⁰ of the bank, neutralize the controls at 60⁰, and then return to level flight.

notes.text: Normal law: the roll rate is proportional to lateral sidestick, up to 15°/s at the stop. Up to 33° the bank holds with the stick neutral; above 33° it returns to 33° when the stick is released, and with full stick held it goes to 67°.
Steep turns above 33°: lateral pressure to keep the bank and aft pressure to stay level.
Alternate law: roll direct law, about 30°/s clean, yaw damping only, no bank angle protection. Above 45° of bank: BANK BANK.

parts.label: Normal law
parts.illustrative: Timing, speed decay, N1 and the rate at which the bank returns to 33° are illustrative.

steps.text: Normal law. 5000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand (A/THR off), flight directors off, bird on. The trainee flies.
Full {left} sidestick. In normal law the roll rate at the stop is about 15°/s.
Past 33° of bank, aft sidestick pressure keeps the aircraft level.
Sidestick neutral at 60°.
Released above 33°, the bank angle protection rolls the aircraft back towards 33°.
Full {right} sidestick: roll rapidly the other way to 60°.
Sidestick neutral at 60°; the bank starts back towards 33°.
Return to level flight.
Wings level. Below 33° the bank holds with the sidestick neutral.

parts.label: Alternate law
parts.illustrative: Timing, sideslip, speed decay and N1 are illustrative.

steps.text: Alternate law: ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3. The protection symbols are now amber x.
Full {left} sidestick. Roll is now direct: about 30°/s clean.
Bank passes 45°: BANK BANK on both PFDs with the "BANK BANK" aural, and the PFD declutters.
Sidestick neutral at 60°. There is no bank angle protection, so the bank stays.
Full {right} sidestick to 60° the other way.
Sidestick neutral at 60°.
Return to level flight.
Wings level.

exercises.title: Roll Rate with rudder input

form.title: Roll Rate with rudder input

exercises.setup: *ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: Roll using only the rudder to 15% of the bank, neutralize the controls at 15% then rapidly roll in the opposite direction to 15* of the bank, neutralize the controls at 150, and then return to level flight.
Maintain approximately level flight and constant airspeed

Large swept-wing transport aircraft are normally not maneuvered with the rudder except for non-normal flight control conditions, takeoff, and landing crosswinds, or when there are asymmetric thrust requirements

Practice using the rudder at different amounts of rudder displacement and rates to see how the airplane reaches, note the roll rate and the controllability difficulty, and the delay of roll and nose movement when the rudder is applied and then the roll due to the sideslip

notes.text: "15%", "15*" and "150" are read as 15° of bank.

The rudder is not normally used to roll a swept-wing transport. The FCTM says it should not be used to induce roll or to counter turbulence, and that aggressive, full or nearly full, opposite rudder pedal inputs must never be applied: against a sideslip they can exceed the limit loads, even below VA, and the rudder travel limiter does not prevent this. The reversal shown is a moderate input.

Alternate law: roll direct, about 30°/s at the stop when clean, and yaw damping only, limited to ±5° of rudder, with no turn coordination. In pitch, alternate law handles as normal law inside the normal envelope, so the sidestick stays neutral.
STOP RUDDER INPUT (red PFD message, aural and MASTER WARN) triggers on inappropriate rudder pedal inputs in cruise at high speed. The books give no thresholds, and it is not shown here.

parts.label: Rudder only
parts.illustrative: Timing, rudder amounts, sideslip, the roll delay and rate, speed, N1 and the trim position are illustrative.

steps.text: Alternate law (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): roll direct, and in yaw only the yaw damping, limited to ±5° of rudder. 5000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand, bird on.
{Left} rudder only. The sidestick stays neutral.
The nose moves first: the aircraft yaws {left}, and the sideslip index moves.
Then the sideslip rolls the aircraft {left}, with a delay.
Rudder neutral as the bank nears 15°.
The sideslip dies away and the bank stays at about 15°. Roll is direct: with the sidestick neutral nothing rolls the wings back.
Rapidly, {right} rudder to roll the other way.
A larger, faster input: the nose swings {right} at once, and the roll follows the sideslip with a delay. Note the roll rate, and how hard it is to stop the roll exactly.
Rudder neutral at about 15° of bank.
Return to level flight with gentle {left} rudder.
Wings level. Altitude and speed stayed close to their starting values throughout.

exercises.title: Pitch Change with the use of only Stabilizer trim

form.title: Pitch Change with the use of only stabilizer trim

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF) and Landing Gear Down

guidance.text: Adjust the stabilizer trim nose high and nose low and note the rate of pitch change and forces.
Pitch rate change occurs slowly because the stabilizer trim change is slow
Pitch forces can be considerable after large stabilizer movements
During a low-speed condition, or a very high-speed condition, there may not be enough elevator authority to recover the airplane to a stable condition

notes.text: Direct law: elevator deflection is proportional to sidestick deflection and there is no automatic trim, so USE MAN PITCH TRIM shows on the PFD. The pitch trim wheels drive the stabilizer mechanically, with priority over electrical trim.

The sidesticks are spring-loaded to neutral and get no feedback from the control surfaces. On the A320 the "pitch forces" of the guidance show as how far the sidestick must be held to keep the attitude.
Stabilizer travel is 13.5° nose up to 4° nose down; elevator travel is 30° nose up and 17° nose down.
The books give no stabilizer rate for the pitch trim wheel, so the trim rate and positions here are illustrative.

parts.label: Stabilizer trim only
parts.illustrative: Timing, the trim rate and positions, load factor, drag, thrust and N1 are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. The books give no stabilizer rate.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down). 5000 ft, 220 kt, thrust set by hand (A/THR off), bird on. USE MAN PITCH TRIM on the FMA: there is no automatic trim.
Sidestick neutral. Trim nose up with the pitch trim wheel.
The nose starts up only slowly: the stabilizer moves slowly, so the pitch rate builds slowly. The aircraft climbs and the speed falls.
Trim nose down, past the original setting.
The nose comes down, again slowly, and the speed builds back.
Trim back to the original setting.
Level again near 5000 ft and 220 kt.
Now trim nose up a long way while holding the attitude with forward sidestick.

The further the stabilizer moves, the further forward the sidestick must be held. The sidesticks are spring-loaded and get no feedback from the control surfaces, so on the A320 this deflection is the "pitch force" of the guidance.
Much of the elevator travel now only holds the attitude, so less is left to manoeuvre. At very low or very high speed there may not be enough elevator authority to recover.

exercises.title: Pitch Change with the use of Thrust Adjustments

form.title: Pitch Change with the use of thrust adjustments

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF) and Landing Gear Down

guidance.text: From a stabilized power setting, rapidly add full power and note the pitch change at this low speed. From a stabilized power setting, reduce thrust rapidly to idle.
Underwing-mounted engines will induce a significant nose-up pitch with power addition on most models
This pitch-up would be even more significant at an even lower speed and less significant at higher speeds

notes.text: All Airbus engines are under the wing: a thrust increase pitches the nose up and a thrust decrease pitches it down.
In direct law be careful with large thrust changes, especially with an aft CG: TOGA thrust gives a large pitch-up moment, so apply nose-down trim accordingly.
F/CTL DIRECT LAW procedure: use manual pitch trim and manoeuvre with care; manual thrust is recommended, avoiding large thrust changes.

parts.label: Full thrust
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1 and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down). 5000 ft, 240 kt, thrust stabilized by hand (A/THR off), bird on, trimmed.
From the stabilized setting, thrust levers rapidly to TOGA. Sidestick neutral: note the pitch change.
The engines are under the wing, so the thrust increase pitches the nose up. In direct law nothing compensates.
At a lower speed this pitch-up would be larger; at a higher speed, smaller.
Forward sidestick to stop the pitch-up and bring the aircraft back to level flight.
Nose-down trim to take the load off the sidestick.
Level and trimmed at TOGA thrust; the speed builds. With the landing gear down, VLE is 280 kt.

parts.label: Idle thrust
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1 and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down). 5000 ft, 240 kt, thrust stabilized by hand (A/THR off), bird on, trimmed.
From the stabilized setting, thrust levers rapidly to IDLE. Sidestick neutral: note the pitch change.
The thrust decrease pitches the nose down.
Aft sidestick to stop the nose-down pitch and bring the aircraft back to level flight.
Nose-up trim to take the load off the sidestick. At idle the speed falls, so level flight needs more and more nose-up trim.
Level again and trimmed nose up; at idle the speed keeps falling.

exercises.title: Pitch change with the use of speed brakes

form.title: Pitch Change with the use of Speed brakes

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF) and Landing Gear Down

guidance.text: From a stabilized condition, rapidly deploy the flight spoilers.
Normally, the deployment of speed brakes will cause the airplane to pitch up (note PRIM 1+2+3 affects spoiler availability and may show little effect)
This usually becomes more pronounced as speed increases

notes.text: The guidance mentions PRIM 1+2+3, but the A320 has no PRIMs: SEC 1, 2 and 3 control its spoilers. On HS-TXA the speedbrakes are spoilers 2, 3 and 4. Extension is inhibited when SEC 1 and SEC 3 are both faulty, an elevator is faulty, the angle-of-attack protection is active, the flaps are at FULL, a thrust lever is above MCT, or alpha floor is active. None of these applies here.

Speedbrakes pitch the nose up; the AP and normal law compensate, but in direct law the pilot must. Avoid sudden speedbrake movements in direct law: with the speedbrakes out and the aircraft re-trimmed, retract them gently to give time to re-trim and avoid a large nose-down trim change.
F/CTL DIRECT LAW procedure: at high Mach numbers, use the speedbrakes with care to avoid too strong nose-up changes.

parts.label: Speedbrakes
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, speedbrake drag, thrust, N1 and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down). 5000 ft, 270 kt, thrust set by hand (A/THR off), bird on, trimmed.
From the stabilized condition, speedbrake lever rapidly to FULL.
The speedbrakes (spoilers 2, 3 and 4) extend: the nose pitches up and the speed starts to fall. In normal law the law and the AP would compensate; in direct law nothing does.
The faster the aircraft, the stronger this pitch-up. At high Mach, use the speedbrakes with care.
Forward sidestick to stop the pitch-up and return to level flight, and nose-down trim to take the load off.
Level and trimmed with the speedbrakes out; the speed keeps falling slowly.

exercises.title: Yaw motion and resultant roll due to asymmetric thrust with autopilot

form.title: Yaw motion and resultant roll due to asymmetric thrust with autopilot

guidance.text: From a stabilized condition with the autopilot on reduce thrust rapidly to idle on one engine.
Note the autopilot's attempt to control roll and the decaying condition with airspeed reducing
Note the small forces and necessary inputs after disconnecting the autopilot

notes.text: Flown with AP2 in HDG and ALT with the flight director bars shown.

With the AP engaged the FMGS sends the rudder trim orders, which compensate an engine failure over the longer term in every guidance mode. The rudder trim moves the neutral point of the pedal feel, so the pedals move with it; yaw damping and turn coordination do not move the pedals. After the AP disconnects, the trim stays where the AP left it until the RUD TRIM RESET pushbutton returns it to zero at 1.5°/s.
In normal law with all protections, the AP disengages when the angle-of-attack or high speed protection activates, or beyond 25° nose up, 13° nose down or 45° of bank.

The normal way to disconnect the AP is the takeover pushbutton pressed twice: the first press gives the AP OFF memo, the cavalry charge and MASTER WARN; the second clears them. Disconnecting with the sidestick or the rudder pedals is to be avoided.
The FD bars show the FD orders in green with HDG V/S as the basic reference; they disappear beyond 45° of bank, 25° up or 13° down.

parts.label: Asymmetric thrust, AP on
parts.illustrative: Timing, the roll and sideslip transients, the rudder trim amount, speed, N1, pitch trim positions and the flight director orders are illustrative.

steps.text: Normal law. AP2 flying in HDG and ALT with the flight directors on; A/THR off, thrust set by hand. 5000 ft, 220 kt.
From a stabilized condition, {eng1} thrust lever rapidly to IDLE.
The thrust asymmetry yaws the aircraft towards the idle engine and starts a roll {left}. The autopilot works to stop the roll and get back to the heading.
The AP's rudder trim moves the rudder pedals {right}: long-term yaw compensation.
Wings level on the heading again, but the speed keeps falling: with A/THR off and one engine at idle, the AP holds the altitude at the expense of speed.
Below green dot, with the pitch attitude rising as the speed decays. Left alone, the AP would disengage when the angle-of-attack protection activates.
Takeover pushbutton on the F/O sidestick: the AP disengages and AP2 leaves the FMA. The cavalry charge sounds, MASTER WARN lights and the AP OFF memo shows.
Second press: the cavalry charge stops and MASTER WARN goes out.
Hand flying: only small sidestick inputs are needed. The rudder trim stays where the AP left it.

guidance.text: From a stabilized condition, rapidly retard one engine to idle. Recover when reaching 30 of bank. Note the rapid onset of the roll without autopilot input

notes.text: Alternate law: roll direct and yaw damping only, so nothing opposes the roll that the sideslip creates. Asymmetric thrust rolls the aircraft with a slight delay.
Up to full rudder may be used to counter asymmetric thrust. With the slats retracted, little rudder is needed to centre the sideslip.

parts.label: Asymmetric thrust, no AP
parts.illustrative: Timing, the yaw, sideslip and roll build-up, the recovery inputs, speed, N1 and the trim position are illustrative.

steps.text: Alternate law (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): roll direct, yaw damping only. 5000 ft, 220 kt, thrust set by hand, bird on, no autopilot.
From a stabilized condition, {eng1} thrust lever rapidly to IDLE.
The thrust asymmetry yaws the aircraft towards the idle engine; the sideslip index moves.
The sideslip rolls the aircraft {left}, faster and faster. Roll is direct, so nothing holds the bank.
Recover at 30° of bank: {right} sidestick and {right} rudder to wings level.
Wings level. Note how quickly the roll built up without the autopilot.
Hold a little {right} rudder to centre the sideslip index while the thrust stays asymmetric; clean, it takes little rudder.

exercises.title: Approach to Stall Recovery (STALL aural warning) using only Pitch Control

form.title: Approach to stall recovery (Stick Shaker) using only pitch control

exercises.form_note: The topics form says "Stick Shaker"; the session guidance says "STALL aural warning".
exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: Reduce thrust from a stabilized condition and maintain altitude until the stick shaker or airplane buffet is noted.
Recover to previously stabilized airspeed using pitch control only
Although not a recommended technique for recovery, the pilot trainee will note the importance of controlling the angle of attack in order to recover
Check the Angle of attack variation by looking at the difference between FPV and attitude
Note: recovery pitch attitude and altitude loss

notes.text: The photo says "stick shaker". On the A320 the stall warning is the "STALL, STALL" voice with the cricket and the red STALL STALL message on the PFD and MASTER WARN; the books describe no stick shaker.
The books give no stall warning speed. The warning at about 154 kt at 1 g, and the VSW strip, are illustrative.
Low speed stability: from about 5 to 10 kt above the stall warning speed a gentle nose-down demand tends to keep the speed up. The flight crew can override it.
Alpha floor is inoperative in alternate law: nothing adds thrust by itself.

The FCTM stall recovery: the immediate key action is to reduce the angle of attack, with a nose-down pitch order and the wings level. When the stall indications have stopped, increase thrust smoothly and check the speedbrakes retracted; immediate maximum thrust is not appropriate, because the engines spool up slowly and the under-wing engines pitch the nose up. Clean below FL 200, select FLAPS 1 during the flight path recovery.

parts.label: Approach to stall, pitch only
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, the sidestick and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. The stall warning speed is illustrative. Green dot (209 kt) is from the QRH at 64.5 t.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): amber x instead of the protection marks, red and black VSW strip on the speed scale. 5 000 ft at green dot, 209 kt at 64.5 t, A/THR off with thrust set by hand, bird on.
From the stabilized condition, thrust levers to IDLE. Keep the altitude.
Alternate pitch law is a load factor demand, like normal law: with the sidestick neutral the aircraft keeps 1 g, so the flight path stays level as the speed falls, about 1 kt a second.
To keep 1 g at a lower speed the angle of attack must rise: the attitude climbs while the flight path vector stays on the horizon. The gap between them is the angle of attack, about 6° now.
About 10 kt above the stall warning speed the low speed stability starts a gentle nose-down demand. The trainee overrides it with aft sidestick to keep the altitude.
Stall warning at about 154 kt: "STALL, STALL" with the cricket, the red STALL STALL message and MASTER WARN flashing. The gap between FPV and attitude is now about 12°.
Recover with pitch control only: forward sidestick to lower the nose. The thrust levers stay at IDLE.
The angle of attack falls below the warning threshold: the stall warning stops. Controlling the angle of attack is what recovers.
Hold the nose about 3° down. At idle thrust only gravity accelerates the aircraft, so the speed builds slowly.
Approaching 209 kt, raise the nose gently to stop the acceleration.
Back at 209 kt, about 1 550 ft lower. Note the recovery pitch attitude, about 3° nose down, and the altitude loss.
At idle thrust 209 kt can only be kept in a descent: about 4° down with the nose about 2° up.

exercises.title: Fly by Wire qualities

form.title: Fly-by-wire qualities

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: Demonstrate Escape maneuver by applying Full back press on the Stick first in Alternate Law and then in Normal law
In alternate Law the airplane will stall
In normal Law allow the airplane to reach the alpha floor while maintaining a full back pressure bank with 45 of a bank to see how the aircraft responds without stalling
In normal Law demonstrate the overspeed protection by applying full stick FWD (and keeping it FWD) and observing how the airplane reacts

notes.text: The escape manoeuvre is flown with the sidestick only.
Part C starts at 10 000 ft instead of 5 000 ft, so the dive ends well clear of the ground.

Normal law protections: load factor +2.5 g to -1 g clean; pitch 30° up (25° at low speed) and 15° down; angle of attack held at or below α max, close to but below the 1 g stall; α floor usually just after α prot; high speed protection.

Alternate law with reduced protections has the load factor limitation only: no pitch attitude, angle-of-attack or high speed protection, and no α floor. Low speed stability and the stall warning take their place.
Part A stops at the stall, where the photo stops. The FCTM stall recovery: nose-down pitch order to reduce the angle of attack, wings level; when the stall indications stop, increase thrust smoothly.

When the α floor conditions end and the speed is above VLS, TOGA LK replaces A.FLOOR in the flashing amber box and the TOGA thrust stays frozen; disconnect the A/THR to cancel it. Kept with an undue speed increase, TOGA thrust can lead to an overspeed. Leave α prot by easing the sidestick forward.

With the sidestick released, the aircraft overshoots VMO only slightly and flies back towards the envelope; high speed protection ends below VMO. With high speed protection active the bank is limited to 40° and returns to 0° when the sidestick is released, and the AP disconnects at VMO + 15 kt.

parts.label: Alternate law: full back stick
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factor build-up, drag and thrust are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. N1 is scaled to about 58% in level flight, near the QRH level-flight table. The stall warning and stall speeds are illustrative.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): amber x instead of the protection marks, red and black VSW strip on the speed scale. No pitch attitude, angle-of-attack or high speed protection; the load factor limitation remains. 5 000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand at about 58% N1, bird on.
Escape manoeuvre: full back sidestick, and hold it. The thrust stays where it is.
The load factor limitation stops the pull at 2.5 g. At 2.5 g the angle of attack is already high, and the speed falls fast.

Stall warning at about 242 kt and 2.5 g: "STALL, STALL" with the cricket, the red STALL STALL message and MASTER WARN flashing. With more load factor the warning comes at a much higher speed. G LOAD on the SD.
Pitch passes 25° up: the PFD declutters.
Buffet.
Still full back sidestick: alternate law has no angle-of-attack protection, and the angle of attack passes the stall angle of attack. The aircraft stalls.

parts.label: Normal law: full back stick at 45° of bank
parts.illustrative: Timing, the load factor build-up, drag, thrust and the 25° pitch limit at low speed are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. N1 is scaled to about 58% in level flight, near the QRH level-flight table. α prot and α max are illustrative.

steps.text: Normal law with all its protections: green = marks for the bank and pitch limits, amber and black α prot and red α max strips on the speed scale. 5 000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand at about 58% N1 (A/THR off), bird on.
Roll {left} to 45° of bank: full sidestick gives 15°/s. Above 33° the bank needs lateral sidestick held, and aft sidestick keeps the flight level.
45° of bank, level, about 1.4 g.
Full back sidestick, and keep the 45° of bank.

At about 2.2 g the angle of attack reaches α prot: the high angle-of-attack protection takes over. The sidestick now demands angle of attack, and full back stick gives α max, no more. No more nose-up trim, and even full lateral sidestick now holds no more than 45° of bank. G LOAD on the SD.

Alpha floor: full back stick with the angle-of-attack protection active. TOGA thrust whatever the thrust levers: A.FLOOR in a flashing amber box on the FMA, A/THR active, A.FLOOR on the EWD. The thrust levers do not move.
Pitch passes 25° up: the PFD declutters, and the FMA with A.FLOOR goes with it.
Pitch attitude protection holds the nose at about 30° up, less as the speed falls.
No stall: the angle of attack never goes beyond α max, close to but below the 1 g stall. With TOGA thrust the aircraft keeps turning and climbing at a low speed.

parts.label: Normal law: full forward stick
parts.illustrative: Timing, the load factor build-up, how the protection's nose-up order grows with speed, drag, thrust and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. N1 is scaled to about 58% in level flight, near the QRH level-flight table.

steps.text: Normal law with all its protections: green = marks for the bank and pitch limits, amber and black α prot and red α max strips on the speed scale. 10 000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand at about 58% N1 (A/THR off), bird on. The red and black VMAX strip starts at VMO, 350 kt.
Full forward sidestick, and keep it forward.
The load factor drops towards -1 g, the clean limit. Below 0.5 g the automatic pitch trim freezes.
G LOAD on the SD.
Pitch passes 13° down: the PFD declutters.
Pitch attitude protection: the nose stops at 15° down, at the green = mark, though the sidestick stays full forward.
Thrust unchanged and the nose 15° down: the speed builds about 5 kt a second.
VMO + 4 kt: OVERSPEED, a red warning with the continuous repetitive chime and MASTER WARN flashing. Pressing MASTER WARN does not stop it.

VMO + 6 kt, the green = on the speed scale: high speed protection. Above VMO the sidestick's nose-down authority shrinks, and a permanent nose-up order is added. The stabilizer trims no further nose down.
With the sidestick still full forward, the nose comes up by itself.
About VMO + 16 kt: the nose-down authority is zero. That does not mean the aircraft stabilizes at that speed.
G LOAD on the SD.
The speed peaks at about 371 kt, VMO + 21 kt, as the nose passes the horizon, after about 2.2 g in the pull-out.
Sidestick still full forward: the aircraft settles in a shallow descent at about 363 kt, VMO + 13 kt. The OVERSPEED warning goes on.

form.title: Exploring Jet engine performance

exercises.form_note: The topics form calls this "Exploring Jet engine performance".

guidance.text: Use tailwind to decrease speed to V/S, for wind shear demonstration
Use thrust to increase speed by 20 Kts. (Note the timing, unable due to thrust limit)
Increase thrust to MCT and TOGA (Note thrust available)
Use the elevator to descent
Buffet, Spiral dive
From maneuvering above, maintain level flight
Increase bank with level flight
Recovery by decreasing bank
Increase bank to let the pitch drop
Recovery by pull then roll (Note the rapid increase in G-load)
Recovery by roll then pull (Note the difference)

notes.text: "V/S" is read as VLS. Thrust is set by hand: CL, then MCT, then TOGA.
"Max Alt" is taken as FL 370: the books give no REC MAX for 64.5 t. Green dot at FL 370 is 2 × 64.5 + 80 + 17 = 226 kt.
The books give no buffet chart or high-altitude thrust data. VLS above 20 000 ft, the buffet onset, α prot, α max and the thrust are illustrative, shaped by the cited rules.
REC MAX keeps a 0.3 g buffet margin. At the maximum altitude the thrust, speed, buffet, angle-of-attack and bank margins are all at their smallest.
Green dot is the speed for the best lift/drag ratio. Below it a speed loss increases the drag, so the aircraft decelerates further; with maximum thrust the only way to regain speed is to descend.

α prot falls with Mach and at high flight level protects from the buffet boundary. With the sidestick released the aircraft holds α prot, so leaving a turn after entering α prot it may climb. Leave α prot by easing the sidestick forward.
Alpha floor is inhibited above M 0.6: at these Mach numbers no automatic TOGA comes.

FCTM nose low: a high bank angle needs prompt action, as altitude turns into speed; reducing the g-load may improve the roll. Recover level flight at a sufficient speed, avoiding a stall from a premature pull at low speed or excessive g at high speed.

parts.label: Thrust at maximum altitude
parts.illustrative: The tailwind, thrust, N1, drag, VLS above 20 000 ft and the trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: FL 370, normal law, at green dot: 226 kt, M 0.71. Thrust set by hand, A/THR off, level flight. VLS, 223 kt, is only 3 kt below.
Tailwind from the IOS: 16 kt more tailwind in 8 seconds.
The speed falls to VLS, about 217 kt. Up here VLS keeps a 0.2 g margin from the buffet.
Thrust levers to CL, to gain 20 kt.
The speed creeps up by about 0.07 kt a second: 20 kt would take about 4 minutes. Below green dot the drag is higher, and there is little thrust margin.
Thrust levers to MCT.
N1 rises only from 86.0% to 87.1%.
Thrust levers to TOGA.
N1 stays at 87.1%: up here MCT may be the maximum thrust available, and TOGA gives nothing more. The speed still gains only about 0.11 kt a second.
Use the elevator: ease the sidestick forward to a flight path about 3° down.
236 kt, 20 kt above the low point, 22 seconds after the push and about 650 ft lower. Below green dot with maximum thrust, descending is the way to gain speed.

parts.label: Buffet in a turn
parts.illustrative: Roll rates, thrust, drag, the buffet onset, α prot and α max at this Mach are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: 36 300 ft, 237 kt, level after the descent, thrust levers in CL.
Increase the bank slowly, about 3° a second, and keep the flight level.
Beyond 33° of bank: lateral sidestick has to be held, and more aft sidestick keeps the flight level.
At 38° of bank and 1.26 g the angle of attack reaches α prot: at high flight level α prot protects from the buffet boundary. The sidestick now demands angle of attack. No alpha floor above M 0.6.
Buffet, at 40° of bank.

45°: even full back sidestick gives only α max, about 1.38 g, less than the 1.40 g that level flight needs. With α prot active, full lateral sidestick holds no more than 45°. The aircraft sinks and loses speed slowly.
Recovery: decrease the bank, and ease the sidestick forward to leave α prot. With the sidestick free the aircraft would hold α prot and climb as the bank comes off.
Out of the buffet.
Below α prot again.
Wings level, about 10 ft lower.

parts.label: Spiral dive: pull, then roll
parts.illustrative: The bank, roll rates (including how fast the bank comes back to 45° in α prot), the pull, thrust, drag, the buffet onset, α prot and α max at this Mach are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: 36 300 ft, 237 kt, level after the descent, thrust levers in CL.
Increase the bank to about 60°, {left}, and let the pitch drop: no aft sidestick.
60° of bank, lateral sidestick held. Turn compensation ends at 33°, so with no aft sidestick the nose drops into a spiral dive: speed and descent rate build fast.
Nose 4° down, 241 kt, M 0.73, already 240 ft lower.
Pull, then roll: full back sidestick first, keeping the bank.

The load factor rises fast. At only 1.3 g the angle of attack reaches α prot at this Mach, and the pull stops at α max. With α prot active, even full lateral sidestick holds no more than 45° of bank: the bank comes back towards 45°.
Buffet.
G LOAD on the SD.
Then roll wings level with full lateral sidestick, still pulling.
Flight path nearly level: ease the sidestick and level off.
Out of the buffet after about 10 seconds.
Level at about 1 650 ft below the start, 263 kt; up to M 0.77 and 1.6 g on the way.

parts.label: Spiral dive: roll, then pull
parts.illustrative: The bank, roll rates, the pull, thrust, drag, the buffet onset, α prot and α max at this Mach are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: 36 300 ft, 237 kt, level after the descent, thrust levers in CL.
Increase the bank to about 60°, {left}, and let the pitch drop: no aft sidestick.
60° of bank, lateral sidestick held. Turn compensation ends at 33°, so with no aft sidestick the nose drops into a spiral dive: speed and descent rate build fast.
Nose 4° down, 241 kt, M 0.73, already 240 ft lower.
Roll, then pull: roll wings level first with full lateral sidestick, no aft sidestick.
Wings level. Now pull gently, about 1.4 g, back to level flight.
Flight path nearly level: ease the sidestick and level off.
Level at about 1 850 ft below the start, 270 kt; up to M 0.79 and 1.4 g on the way. The difference: no buffet and no α prot, and the load factor stays low.

guidance.text: With validated IOS upset function: Activate the IOS function "(Nose Up 30°)". Without validated IOS upset function: Instructor at pilot seat and apply nose up attitude. Ask the trainee to recognize the situation and apply the recovery technique.
As the airplane pitch attitude passes approximately 40⁰, countering pitch: by use of up to full nose down the elevator and, if required, by using stabilizer trim to relieve elevator control pressure.
A steady nose-down pitch rate should be achieved and noted that the airplane would be near zero g and the associated characteristics of such.
Completes the recovery when approaching the horizon by checking Airspeed, adjusting thrust, and establishing the appropriate pitch attitude and stabilizer trim setting for level flight.

notes.text: Alternate law with the landing gear down becomes direct law: USE MAN PITCH TRIM on the FMA, and pitch trim is by hand.
The instructor flies the entry from the left seat; the trainee counters as the pitch nears 40°. Pitch stays below 40° so the abnormal attitude law does not engage.

No trim in the entry: the instructor raises the nose with the sidestick only. In direct law the elevator follows the sidestick and nothing trims automatically, so the trim stays where it was for the entry speed. In this model, once the sidestick is released, the nose then starts down by itself as the speed falls (illustrative).

FCTM nose high actions: as much nose-down pitch order as needed to get a nose-down pitch rate; if pitch-down authority is short, incremental nose-down trim. Recover level flight at a sufficient speed, avoiding a stall from a premature recovery at low speed.

parts.label: Nose high, nose-down elevator
parts.illustrative: Timing, the sidestick and trim amounts, load factors, drag, thrust and N1 are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down): the sidestick moves the elevator, there is no automatic trim, and USE MAN PITCH TRIM shows on the FMA. 5 000 ft, 270 kt, thrust set by hand at about 70% N1 (A/THR off), bird on.
The instructor pulls on the CAPT sidestick to raise the nose, without trim. (A validated IOS upset function would use "Nose Up 30°".)
G LOAD on the SD.
Pitch passes 25° up: the PFD declutters to attitude, speed, speed trend, heading, altitude and V/S.
Pitch passes 30°: red arrowheads point the nose back to the horizon. Speed is falling fast.
The trainee recognizes the upset, announces it and takes the controls. The instructor lets go.
Up to full forward sidestick as the pitch nears 40° (it peaks at about 38°).
Steady nose-down pitch rate, close to zero g (about 0.1 g).
Nose-down trim to relieve the elevator pressure. Trim is manual in direct law.
Pitch below 22°: the full PFD returns.
Approaching the horizon at about 187 kt: check the speed, add thrust, set the pitch attitude and trim for level flight.
Thrust levers to CL.
Nose-up trim for level flight at the lower speed.
Level flight at about 6 870 ft, 1 870 ft above the entry; speed increasing.

form.title: Exercise 2 Nose High Iteration 2: Use of Bank Angle

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF) and Landing Gear Down

guidance.text: With validated IOS upset function: Activate the IOS function "(Nose Up 30°)". Without validated IOS upset function: Instructor at pilot seat and apply nose up attitude. Ask the trainee to recognize the situation and apply the recovery technique.

Roll the airplane until a nose-down pitch rate is achieved. Some forward Sidestick pressure may be required. 30 to 60 banks should be sufficient to establish a nose-down pitch rate. Avoid bank angles over 60⁰.

notes.text: Flown with 45° of bank.
Alternate law with the landing gear down becomes direct law: roll is direct and nothing limits the bank; above 45° the PFD would show BANK BANK.

No trim in the entry: the instructor raises the nose with the sidestick only. In direct law the elevator follows the sidestick and nothing trims automatically, so the trim stays where it was for the entry speed. In this model, once the sidestick is released, the nose then starts down by itself as the speed falls (illustrative).

FCTM nose high actions: if all normal pitch control techniques are unsuccessful, bank the aircraft to let the nose drop towards the horizon; the least bank that starts the nose down, never more than about 60°. The guidance stops here; the FCTM then recovers level flight at a sufficient speed.

parts.label: Nose high, bank angle
parts.illustrative: Timing, the sidestick and trim amounts, load factors, drag, thrust and N1 are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. The demonstration stops where the guidance stops, once the nose-down pitch rate is achieved.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down): the sidestick moves the elevator, there is no automatic trim, and USE MAN PITCH TRIM shows on the FMA. 5 000 ft, 270 kt, thrust set by hand at about 70% N1 (A/THR off), bird on.
The instructor pulls on the CAPT sidestick to raise the nose, without trim. (A validated IOS upset function would use "Nose Up 30°".)
G LOAD on the SD.
Pitch passes 25° up: the PFD declutters to attitude, speed, speed trend, heading, altitude and V/S.
Pitch passes 30°: red arrowheads point the nose back to the horizon. Speed is falling fast.
The trainee recognizes the upset, announces it and takes the controls. The instructor lets go.
Roll {left} towards 45° of bank, with some forward sidestick pressure. Roll is direct: about a third of the lateral sidestick here.
45° of bank, held with the sidestick about neutral: in direct law nothing rolls the wings back. The guidance says to avoid more than 60°.
With the lift tilted, the nose falls faster: a nose-down pitch rate of about 4°/s.

exercises.title: EXERCISE 3. Nose High Iteration 3- Thrust Reduction (Underwing-Mounted Engines)

form.title: Exercise 3 Nose High Iteration 3: Thrust Reduction (Underwing Mounted Engines)

exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF) and Landing Gear Down

guidance.text: With validated IOS upset function: Activate the IOS function "(Nose Up 30°)". Without validated IOS upset function: Instructor at pilot seat and apply nose up attitude. Ask the trainee to recognize the situation and apply the recovery technique.
Recovery by reducing thrust to approximately midrange until a detectable nose-down pitch rate is achieved.
Completes the recovery when approaching the horizon by checking airspeed, adjusting thrust, and establishing the appropriate pitch attitude and stabilizer trim setting for level flight.

notes.text: Thrust levers at CL during the upset, then back to halfway between IDLE and CL.
The trainee acts as the pitch reaches about 30°, the attitude the IOS "Nose Up 30°" function gives.

No trim in the entry: the instructor raises the nose with the sidestick only. In direct law the elevator follows the sidestick and nothing trims automatically, so the trim stays where it was for the entry speed. In this model, once the sidestick is released, the nose then starts down by itself as the speed falls (illustrative).
Engines under the wing: a thrust increase pitches the nose up and a decrease pitches it down; in direct law nothing compensates.

FCTM nose high actions: increasing thrust may reduce the nose-down pitch control; it may be necessary to limit or reduce thrust until pitch control is achieved. Recover level flight at a sufficient speed, avoiding a stall from a premature recovery at low speed.

parts.label: Nose high, thrust reduction
parts.illustrative: Timing, the sidestick and trim amounts, load factors, drag, thrust and N1 are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down): the sidestick moves the elevator, there is no automatic trim, and USE MAN PITCH TRIM shows on the FMA. 5 000 ft, 250 kt, thrust set by hand at about 64% N1 (A/THR off), bird on.
The instructor sets the thrust levers to CL and pulls on the CAPT sidestick to raise the nose, without trim. (A validated IOS upset function would use "Nose Up 30°".)
G LOAD on the SD.
Pitch passes 25° up: the PFD declutters to attitude, speed, speed trend, heading, altitude and V/S.
The trainee recognizes the upset, announces it and takes the controls. The instructor lets go.
Thrust levers back to about mid-range, halfway between IDLE and CL. Sidestick neutral.
The engines are under the wing, so less thrust pitches the nose down; with the sidestick neutral the falling speed helps too: a detectable nose-down pitch rate.
Pitch below 22°: the full PFD returns.
Approaching the horizon at about 176 kt: check the speed, adjust the thrust, set the pitch attitude and trim for level flight.
Thrust levers to CL.
The speed is low: the nose stays near the horizon while the speed builds, then nose-up trim for level flight. No premature recovery at low speed.
Level flight, speed increasing.

form.title: Exercise 4 Nose Low Iteration 4: Nose Low Recovery

guidance.text: With validated IOS upset function: Activate the IOS function "Nose Down -20° & Bank 70° (left or right)".
Without validated IOS upset function:
Pull up gently to 20⁰ nose up and then start to slowly roll the aircraft while allowing the nose to drop.

Observe the nose drop and airspeed increase and the outside view change to mostly ground with just a 10 to 20° nose-low altitude. Aim for approximately 20⁰, nose low, and 60 to 70⁰ of a bank before initiating recovery.

Ask the trainee to recognize the situation and apply the recovery technique. Recover by recognizing and confirming the situation; verifying that the autopilot and auto thrust are disengaged; rolling to approaching wings level, then applying nose up elevator; and adjusting thrust and drag as necessary.

notes.text: The demonstration flies the entry without the IOS function, as in the second guidance option. The IOS function sets about 20° nose down and 70° of bank directly.

Your decision: this row follows physics. At 65° of bank the lift no longer holds the nose up, so it keeps dropping while the wings roll level: from about 20° nose low it passes 20° down, and with one valid ADC (ADR 1+2 OFF) the abnormal attitude law engages.

parts.label: Nose-low recovery
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, lever and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. Green dot (209 kt) is from the QRH at 64.5 t.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): roll direct, amber x instead of the protection marks. 5 000 ft at green dot, 209 kt at 64.5 t, A/THR off with thrust set by hand, bird on.
Entry without the IOS function: the instructor pulls up gently on the CAPT sidestick towards 20° nose up. Thrust unchanged: the speed bleeds off in the climb.
At about 20° nose up, start a slow roll to the {left} and let the nose drop with a little forward pressure.
Bank passes 45°: BANK BANK on the PFD with the "BANK BANK" aural (alternate law); the PFD declutters.
Bank held at about 65°: the nose drops and the speed builds again, and the view outside turns to mostly ground. Aim for about 20° nose low and 60 to 70° of bank.
At about 20° nose low the trainee takes the controls on the F/O sidestick; the instructor lets go.
Recognize and confirm the situation; the FMA shows AP and A/THR off.

The nose passes 20° down. With one valid ADC this engages the abnormal attitude law: MASTER CAUT, single chime, ECAM F/CTL DIRECT LAW. Pitch alternate with no protection (no load factor limitation) and no autotrim (USE MAN PITCH TRIM), roll direct, yaw mechanical.
Full {right} sidestick: roll to approaching wings level. Roll is direct, about 30°/s at most when clean. With the wings still banked the nose keeps dropping, to about 22° down.
Approaching wings level: nose-up elevator, about 1.7 g, avoiding the stall warning.

Nose back above 20° down: the abnormal attitude law disengages. For the rest of the flight: pitch alternate law without reduced protection (load factor limitation only), roll direct, yaw alternate, and F/CTL ALTN LAW on the ECAM, a new amber caution: MASTER CAUT and a single chime again. Autotrim works again. When it disengages is assumed: the books give no values.
G LOAD on the SD: above 1.4 g for more than 2 s. Pitch back above 10° down with the wings level: the full PFD returns.
Ease the back pressure as the flight path comes level at about 4 050 ft.
About 245 kt, well above green dot: thrust to idle while the speed comes back, then set thrust for level flight.
Level flight at about 4 050 ft; the speed settles back towards green dot.

exercises.title: Exercise 5. Nose Low Iteration 2- Accelerated Stall

form.title: Exercise 5 Nose Low: Iteration 5: Accelerated Stall Demonstration

exercises.form_note: The topics form numbers the nose-low iterations 4, 5 and 6; the session guidance numbers them 1, 2 and 3.
exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: Instructor at pilot seat:
Apply nose-up an elevator and some small amount of nose-up stabilizer trim to slowly achieve approximately a 20⁰ nose-up pitch. Do not change the entry thrust.
Upon reaching approximately a 20⁰ nose-up pitch, roll the airplane to approximately 90⁰ bank and allow the nose to fall.

Ask the trainee to recognize the situation: When slightly nose low and at minimal airspeed, apply sufficient backpressure until achieving stick shaker. Note the airspeed then unload to eliminate the stick shaker.
Ask the trainee to apply the recovery technique:

The bank will be maintained and airspeed allowed to increase. At a high airspeed, once again have the pilot trainee apply sufficient backpressure until achieving stick shaker. Note the airspeed, then unload and initiate recovery.

Recovery is accomplished by recognizing and confirming the situation and verifying that the autopilot and auto thrust are disengaged. The trainee rolls to approaching wings level and then recovers to level flight by applying nose up elevator, if necessary, and adjusting thrust and drag as necessary.

notes.text: The photo says "stick shaker". On the A320 the stall warning is the "STALL, STALL" voice with the cricket and the red STALL STALL message on the PFD and MASTER WARN; the books describe no stick shaker.

FCTM nose low actions: reducing the g-loading may improve roll effectiveness; reduce thrust and/or use the speedbrakes to control the speed; recover avoiding a stall at low speed or excessive g at high speed.
The books give no stall warning speeds. The speeds where the warning sounds, about 161 kt at 1.1 g and about 213 kt at 1.9 g, and the VSW strip rising with load factor, are illustrative.

Your decision: this row follows physics. At about 90° of bank the lift is horizontal, so the nose falls 5 to 7° a second whatever the stick does; holding the bank while the speed builds takes the nose about 45° down. Past 20° down, with one valid ADC, the abnormal attitude law engages.
Low speed stability: from about 5 to 10 kt above the stall warning speed a gentle nose-down demand tends to keep the speed up. The trainee overrides it to load the aircraft to the warning.

parts.label: Accelerated stall
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, lever and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. Green dot (209 kt) is from the QRH at 64.5 t.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): roll direct, amber x instead of the protection marks. 10 000 ft at green dot, 209 kt at 64.5 t, thrust set by hand, bird on.
The instructor pulls gently on the CAPT sidestick and adds a little nose-up trim, slowly towards 20° nose up. Entry thrust unchanged: the speed bleeds off in the climb.
At about 20° nose up, roll to about 90° of bank and let the nose fall.
Bank passes 45°: BANK BANK on the PFD with the "BANK BANK" aural (alternate law); the PFD declutters.
The trainee takes the controls on the F/O sidestick; the instructor lets go. The nose passes the horizon at the lowest speed, about 160 kt.
Slightly nose low at minimal airspeed: a little back pressure.
Stall warning at about 161 kt and 1.1 g: "STALL, STALL" with the cricket, the red STALL STALL message and MASTER WARN flashing. Note the speed.
Unload: the warning stops.

The nose passes 20° down. With one valid ADC this engages the abnormal attitude law: MASTER CAUT, single chime, ECAM F/CTL DIRECT LAW. Pitch alternate with no protection (no load factor limitation) and no autotrim (USE MAN PITCH TRIM), roll direct, yaw mechanical.
Bank kept at 90°: the lift is horizontal, so the nose keeps falling whatever the stick does, and the speed builds fast.
At a high airspeed, pull again until the stall warning.
Stall warning again at about 213 kt and 1.9 g: with more load factor the warning comes at a higher speed, and the VSW strip rises with it.
Note the speed, then unload and start the recovery.
Recognize and confirm the situation; AP and A/THR are off. Thrust levers to IDLE and speedbrakes out to control the speed.
Unloaded, full {right} sidestick rolls towards wings level. Roll is direct: about 30°/s at most when clean.
Near wings level: nose-up elevator, about 2.4 g, to bring the nose back up without overspeed.

Nose back above 20° down: the abnormal attitude law disengages. For the rest of the flight: pitch alternate law without reduced protection (load factor limitation only), roll direct, yaw alternate, and F/CTL ALTN LAW on the ECAM, a new amber caution: MASTER CAUT and a single chime again. Autotrim works again. When it disengages is assumed: the books give no values.
G LOAD on the SD: above 1.4 g for more than 2 s.
Pitch back above 10° down with the wings level: the full PFD returns.
Level off at about 6 200 ft; idle thrust and speedbrakes while the speed comes back.
Speedbrakes in; thrust set for level flight.
Level flight, about 265 kt.

exercises.form_note: The topics form numbers the nose-low iterations 4, 5 and 6; the session guidance numbers them 1, 2 and 3.
exercises.setup: ADR 1+2 OFF and AIR DATA SWITCHING to CAPT or FO on "3" (to PF)

guidance.text: With validated IOS upset function: Activate the IOS function "Nose Down -20° & Bank 110-120° (left or right)". Without validated IOS upset function: Roll the airplane slowly to achieve approximately 110 to 120 of bank and approximately 20 nose low.

Ask the trainee to recognize the situation and apply the recovery technique: When approximately 20 below the horizon, the trainee recovers by recognizing and confirming the situation and verifying that the autopilot and auto thrust are disengaged. The trainee must unload and roll, when approaching wings level, recover to level flight by applying nose-up elevator and nose-up stabilizer trim, if necessary, and adjust thrust and drag as necessary.

notes.text: The demonstration flies the entry without the IOS function. The IOS function sets about 20° nose down and 110 to 120° of bank directly.

The guidance asks for a slow roll, but with your decision to follow physics the roll rate decides the entry: from level flight a 6°/s roll reaches 115° of bank with the nose about 40° down. The demonstration rolls at about 15°/s (illustrative) to arrive near 20° nose low.

Your decision: this row follows physics. Beyond 90° of bank the lift points below the horizon, so the nose passes 20° down, and with one valid ADC (ADR 1+2 OFF) the abnormal attitude law engages. The bank stays below 125°.

parts.label: High bank recovery
parts.illustrative: Timing, roll rates, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, lever and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. Green dot (209 kt) is from the QRH at 64.5 t.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): roll direct, amber x instead of the protection marks. 10 000 ft at green dot, 209 kt at 64.5 t, A/THR off with thrust set by hand, bird on.
Entry without the IOS function: the instructor rolls to the {left} on the CAPT sidestick, a steady roll of about 15°/s towards 110 to 120° of bank.
Bank passes 45°: BANK BANK on the PFD with the "BANK BANK" aural (alternate law); the PFD declutters.
Past 90° of bank the lift points below the horizon: the nose drops fast whatever the stick does.
At about 115° of bank and 20° nose low the trainee takes the controls on the F/O sidestick; the instructor lets go.
Recognize and confirm the situation; the FMA shows AP and A/THR off.

The nose passes 20° down. With one valid ADC this engages the abnormal attitude law: MASTER CAUT, single chime, ECAM F/CTL DIRECT LAW. Pitch alternate with no protection (no load factor limitation) and no autotrim (USE MAN PITCH TRIM), roll direct, yaw mechanical.
Unload: forward sidestick to about 0.3 g. Reducing the g-loading may improve roll effectiveness.
Thrust levers to IDLE and speedbrakes out to control the speed.
Full {right} sidestick: roll the shortest way to wings level, back through 90°. Roll is direct, about 30°/s at most when clean; the nose keeps dropping, to about 32° down.
G LOAD on the SD: below 0.7 g for more than 2 s.
Approaching wings level: nose-up elevator, about 2.3 g, avoiding excessive g at this speed.

Nose back above 20° down: the abnormal attitude law disengages. For the rest of the flight: pitch alternate law without reduced protection (load factor limitation only), roll direct, yaw alternate, and F/CTL ALTN LAW on the ECAM, a new amber caution: MASTER CAUT and a single chime again. Autotrim works again, so no nose-up trim by hand is needed. When it disengages is assumed: the books give no values.
Pitch back above 10° down with the wings level: the full PFD returns.
Ease the back pressure as the flight path comes level at about 7 900 ft.
Speedbrakes in; thrust set for level flight.
Level flight at about 7 900 ft, about 250 kt.

exercises.title: Exercise 7. Nose-High Low energy

form.title: Exercise 7: Nose-High Low energy

exercises.form_note: The topics form shows no autopilot and the bird; the session guidance has AP/FD ON.

guidance.text: Maintain thrust on another engine (S), hold the throttle in idle against auto thrust commands until recovery is initiated. In certain envelope-protected airplanes, certain features may have to be disabled to allow this scenario to work.
Observe the developing yaw and roll condition and decreasing airspeed.
Disengaging the autopilot and auto thrust, and applying appropriate recovery techniques. Roll control may require as much as full aileron and spoiler input and the use of a coordinated rudder.
After recovery, normal thrust is used and training continues.

notes.text: Animated as the photo describes, with the yaw, roll and speed decay developing with the autopilot on. This assumes protections inhibited at the IOS; it is not FCOM behaviour.

By the FCOM the aircraft would not do this with the AP on: SRS holds V2 + 10 kt with the pitch, the AP's rudder trim gives long-term yaw compensation after an engine failure, the lateral normal law commands rudder against a thrust asymmetry, and alpha floor stays available.

At 1 000 ft the thrust is taken as already reduced to CL (THR CLB, A/THR active), so the A/THR is commanding thrust as the guidance describes. The FCTM default thrust reduction altitude is 1 500 ft; below it the levers would still be at TOGA or FLX with the A/THR only armed.
Radio height on the PFD below 2 500 ft: the ground is taken at sea level, so it equals the altitude (illustrative).
The β target needs an EPR above 1.25: the EPR in CL is assumed to be above 1.25 (the books give no EPR values).
V2 = 140 kt is illustrative: the books give no takeoff speeds at 64.5 t.

FCTM, engine failure at takeoff: follow the SRS orders, which may ask for a lower pitch to get the target speed; the lateral normal law gives only part of the rudder, so centre the β target with the pedals; control the heading with bank; then trim the rudder and engage the AP.

parts.label: Thrust asymmetry with the autopilot on
parts.illustrative: Timing, the climb gradient, V2 (140 kt), drag, thrust, N1 and EPR, the sideslip, rudder, sidestick and trim amounts are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them.

steps.text: Normal law, CONF 1+F, landing gear up: climbing through 1 000 ft after takeoff at V2 + 10 kt, 150 kt. AP2 in SRS and NAV, CLB armed, flight directors on. A/THR active in THR CLB, both thrust levers in CL. The magenta speed target shows V2.
Thrust lever {eng1} to IDLE, and held there. The other engine keeps its thrust.

The A320's thrust levers do not move with the A/THR. With one lever in CL and the other at IDLE the A/THR stays active in THR CLB: the IDLE lever limits its engine to idle. No LVR ASYM with a lever at IDLE.
The EPRs are now more than 0.25 apart with the flap lever in 1: the sideslip index turns blue, the β target. It sits off centre: nobody is correcting the yaw.
The yaw builds and the aircraft rolls {left}. With less thrust and the pitch attitude held, the speed falls, about 1.5 kt a second.
The SRS pitch bar asks for a lower pitch to keep V2 + 10 kt and the roll bar for wings level, but the AP does not follow: here its protections are inhibited at the IOS.
At about 15° of bank and 141 kt: takeover pushbutton on the F/O sidestick. AP2 disengages: AP OFF memo, cavalry charge, MASTER WARN.
Full {right} sidestick to roll the wings level, and {right} rudder, coordinated. At the stop the roll rate is 15°/s.
Second press: the cavalry charge stops, MASTER WARN goes out and the AP OFF memo clears.
Wings level. Rudder to centre the β target; the nose is lowered to follow the SRS order and stop the speed decay, without descending this close to the ground.
A/THR instinctive disconnect pushbutton: A/THR leaves the FMA, and each engine now gives the thrust its lever sets. Amber A/THR OFF memo, MASTER CAUT and a single chime.
Recovered: normal thrust, thrust lever {eng1} back to CL. With the A/THR off, both engines give CL thrust.
The EPRs come back together: the β target becomes the yellow sideslip index again. Rudder back to neutral as the engine spools up.
Back near V2 + 10 kt and climbing, the SRS pitch bar centred. Training continues.

exercises.title: Exercise 8. High Altitude Stall Warning

form.title: Exercise 8: High Altitude Stall Warning

exercises.form_note: The topics form ticks AP and A/THR with FD; the session guidance has OFF (Bird ON).

guidance.text: Begins this lesson on a cruise flight with an airplane at an altitude of FL250 or above. The airplane weight should be at or near that altitude's maximum based on the company or manufacturer's procedures. Initially STD QNH and OAT=ISA.
Simulating upset conditions leading to high-altitude stalls, varying conditions such as different entry attitudes, thrust levels, or turbulence.

High-Altitude Stall Recovery: Immediate actions to reduce AOA (nose down); Controlled application of thrust (avoid overcorrecting); Managing aircraft energy throughout the recovery process; Re-establishing level flight

notes.text: Flown in alternate law (ADR 1+2 OFF) instead of the table's Normal. Entry: thrust reduced while holding altitude.
"Max Alt" is flown as FL 370: the books give no recommended maximum altitude at 64.5 t.
The FCOM recovery starts as soon as any stall indication is recognized, the buffet included. Here the entry goes on to the stall warning, as briefed for this exercise.
Low speed stability: from about 5 to 10 kt above the stall warning speed a gentle nose-down demand tends to keep the speed up. The flight crew can override it.
Alpha floor is inoperative in alternate law: nothing adds thrust by itself.

FCTM stall recovery: reduce the angle of attack first; when the stall indications have stopped, increase thrust smoothly. Immediate maximum thrust is not appropriate: the engines spool up slowly and the under-wing engines pitch the nose up. No FLAPS 1 above FL 200.

parts.label: High altitude stall warning
parts.illustrative: Timing, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, the sidestick and trim positions are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. The buffet and stall warning angles of attack at high Mach are illustrative. Green dot is from the FCOM rule at 64.5 t.

steps.text: Alternate law with reduced protections (ADR 1+2 OFF, AIR DATA SWITCHING on F/O 3): amber x instead of the protection marks, red and black VSW strip on the speed scale. FL 370 at green dot, 226 kt (M 0.71) at 64.5 t, STD, A/THR off with thrust set by hand, bird on.
Thrust levers to IDLE, and keep FL 370.
Up here the indicated speed falls slowly, about 0.7 kt a second: the true airspeed is much higher than the indicated one. To keep 1 g the angle of attack, and the attitude, rise.
About 10 kt above the stall warning speed the low speed stability starts a gentle nose-down demand. The trainee overrides it to keep the altitude.
Buffet at about 183 kt, M 0.58. At this Mach number it comes just before the stall warning: the warning is set close to the buffet angle of attack, and both fall as the Mach number rises.
Stall warning at about 178 kt: "STALL, STALL" with the cricket, the red STALL STALL message and MASTER WARN flashing.
Immediate action: nose down to reduce the angle of attack, wings level. The thrust stays at IDLE for now.
The angle of attack falls below the threshold: the stall warning stops, and the buffet with it.
Out of the stall: thrust levers smoothly to CL, no further. Check the speedbrakes retracted.
Manage the energy: hold a shallow descent, about 3° down, while the speed builds back to green dot. With little thrust margin up here, descending is how to regain speed.
Back at green dot: raise the nose smoothly to level flight.
Level again at about FL 349, 2 100 ft below the entry.

exercises.title: Exercise 9: Landing Configuration stall

form.title: Exercise 9: Landing Configuration stall

exercises.form_note: The session guidance gives no conditions table for this exercise; the title is from the topics form.

guidance.text: Set airplane to 2000 ft. on ILS
Arm APP with thrust idle
Demonstrate stall at low altitude and recovery

notes.text: Flown with ADR 1+2 OFF and the landing gear down (direct law), CONF FULL. The autopilot is not available in direct law, so APP cannot be armed.
On the ILS: the PFD shows ILS raw data with the LS pushbutton pressed, the localizer and glideslope deviation scales, the ILS ident, frequency and DME, and the course pointer.

The ILS geometry is illustrative: a 3° glideslope, a start 7 NM from the touchdown point on the localizer, the ground at sea level (so the radio height equals the altitude), the DME read from the touchdown point, and the ident and frequency from the FCOM figure. The glideslope deviation stays inside one dot, so the scale never flashes.
The books give no stall warning speed: the warning at about 1.03 times the 1 g stall speed, and the VSW strip, are illustrative.

FCOM stall recovery: as soon as any stall indication is recognized, nose down pitch control and wings level; when out of the stall, increase thrust smoothly as needed, check the speedbrakes retracted and recover the flight path smoothly. If a risk of ground contact exists, once clearly out of the stall, establish smoothly a positive climb gradient.
Thrust to CL in the recovery.

In direct law, care with large thrust changes: the FCTM warns that TOGA gives a large pitch-up, to be trimmed nose down. CL gives a smaller pitch-up, still countered here with forward sidestick and nose-down trim.

parts.label: Landing configuration stall
parts.illustrative: Timing, the start speed, load factors, drag, thrust, N1, the sidestick and trim amounts are illustrative; speed, flight path and altitude follow from them. The stall warning speed is illustrative.

steps.text: Direct law (ADR 1+2 OFF with the landing gear down): the sidestick moves the elevator, there is no automatic trim, and USE MAN PITCH TRIM shows on the FMA. CONF FULL, landing gear down, 2 000 ft on the ILS at 140 kt, thrust set by hand, bird on. The AP, FD and A/THR are not available, so APP cannot be armed.
ILS raw data: on the localizer, and below the glideslope, so its magenta diamond sits above the centre, about 0.8 dot. Radio height in green.
Thrust levers to IDLE. Keep 2 000 ft: aft sidestick, and nose-up trim by hand as the speed falls.
In the landing configuration the drag is high: the speed falls about 2.1 kt a second.
Below VLS, 134 kt. The red and black VSW strip is close.
Stall warning at about 113 kt: "STALL, STALL" with the cricket, the red STALL STALL message and MASTER WARN flashing.
Stall recovery, memory items: nose down pitch control, wings level.
Out of the stall: the stall warning stops.
Thrust increased smoothly, here to CL; speedbrakes checked retracted.
The engines are under the wing: the thrust increase pitches the nose up, and in direct law nothing compensates. Forward sidestick and nose-down trim.
Close to the ground: once clearly out of the stall, establish a positive climb gradient smoothly.
Climbing. The lowest point was about 1 680 ft, 320 ft below the entry.
